hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer PandaDoc from a written spec. Claude passed all twenty-nine checks, and found eight gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the quoting part of PandaDoc a small sales team uses. A price list, so prices stay the same. Line items with discounts, tax and live totals. Templates for common packages. And a client link, where the buyer accepts by typing their name.

The core rule is discount approval. Take Lee's quote for Ridgeway Partners. The list price is seventeen thousand, four hundred dollars. Twenty percent off a hundred seats takes off three thousand. That's seventeen point two percent, over the fifteen percent limit, so a manager must approve it before it's sent. And no manager can approve their own quote.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation, with clients, the price list and settings. Quotes and pricing. Approval, sending and the client page. Then expiry, printing and invoices. Every check ran in a real browser, on freshly seeded data.

Here's what it built. The quotes home shows open quotes, approvals waiting, and the win rate. The editor keeps list prices fixed, updates totals live, and warns when a discount needs a manager. The manager sees the approval request beside the quote. Templates make common packages one click. And on a phone, the client accepts by typing their full name.
In the final run, on a fresh database, all twenty-nine checks passed, along with forty-seven automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The build exposed eight gaps in the spec. Places where Claude had to guess. Sign-in matched people by email, but the seed people had no emails. Duplicate didn't say what gets copied, like the discount and notes. And when no other manager could approve, the spec didn't say if the request went through. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test real sign-in, sending email, the daily job on a real scheduler, the browser's print dialog, or hosting. Those are yours to check before a team relies on it.

So is it worth building? PandaDoc Starter is nineteen dollars per seat per month, with up to five templates. Business is forty-nine. For a team of ten on Business, that's five thousand, eight hundred and eighty dollars a year. If you need legally binding e-signatures, payments, or CRM sync, use PandaDoc. If you send a few quotes a week, you mostly need the price list, the approval rule, and an accept link.
Everything is in one file. The data model, sixteen rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all twenty-nine checks, with the eight fixes already in.
